Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

own adjective

my own, one’s own

also my own, your own, his own, her own, of one’s own accord, its own, our own, their own, one’s own

classical

Liv. 2.32.9: singulīs membrīs suum cuique cōnsilium, suus sermō
Plaut. Stich. 1.2.76: suus rēx rēgīnae placet, a queen likes her own king (Lewis & Short)

suus, sua, suum

pronoun (possessive) · Declension on Wiktionary

his, her, its, their own; one’s own

Latin’s “own” is the possessive itself: meus, tuus, noster, vester for the other persons, put first for weight (meā manū, with my own hand: Cic. Sen. 59).

Other words

  • 1proprius: short o (Lewis & Short prō̆prius, marking the o both long and short). De Vaan 490, s.v. prō: short pro- occurs “in some older compounds, such as procul, probus, proprius”. The first syllable is heavy only by position, before pr.

    proprius1, propria, proprium — one’s own, not shared

    adjective · also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 21: tria praedia … propria trāduntur (Lewis & Short); Phaedr. 1.4.1: āmittit meritō proprium quī aliēnum adpetit · Declension on Wiktionary

    The opposite of commūnis: what is yours alone.

  • suā sponte — of one’s own accord

    also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 1.1.50: suā sponte rēctē facere (Lewis & Short); Cic. Fam. 1.7.3 (Lewis & Short)

    meā, tuā sponte for the other persons; in good prose sponte always has the possessive (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • meī sunt ōrdinēs, mea dīscrīptiō, multae etiam istārum arborum meā manū sunt satae

    the rows are mine, the plan is mine, and many of those trees were planted with my own handCic. Sen. 59

  • singulīs membrīs suum cuique cōnsilium, suus sermō fuerit

    each limb had its own mind and its own voiceLiv. 2.32.9

  • āmittit meritō proprium quī aliēnum adpetit

    whoever grabs at what is another’s deserves to lose his ownPhaedr. 1.4.1

See also own, only, his, her, their, oneself.
